summary: Defines a framework for extending SMTP by letting a server tell a client which service extensions it supports. It was a draft standard. It was replaced by RFC 1869.

eli5.summary: Two mail computers introduce themselves and say which extra tricks they know. A newer version replaced it.

subtitle: The EHLO handshake that lets an SMTP server announce which optional features it supports.

tldr.problem: SMTP had no consistent way to add new features, and clients could not tell what an individual server supported.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens with the new EHLO command instead of HELO. An extended server replies with a multiline 250 response that lists a keyword for each extension it supports. Extensions are registered with the IANA, and MAIL FROM and RCPT TO may carry extra parameters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1651 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 1425 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 1869.

today: RFC 1651 is obsoleted by RFC 1869, so that is the RFC to read for the current definition. It was a Draft Standard and itself obsoleted RFC 1425.

sections.title: Why SMTP Needed a Framework
sections.content:
SMTP had been a stable basis for relaying mail for about a decade, but the need for protocol extensions had become clear. Rather than describe each extension as a separate, haphazard addition, RFC 1651 builds a single framework for all future ones. It does not require changes to existing clients or servers unless the new features are actually used.

The RFC is cautious. It says that protocols with few options tend towards ubiquity and protocols with many options tend towards obscurity, so every extension must be weighed against its implementation, deployment and interoperability costs, and in many cases the cost will outweigh the benefit.

The framework has three parts: a new command (EHLO), a registry of SMTP service extensions, and extra parameters on the MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone bolting on their own tricks, there is now one polite way to ask and answer, and the RFC warns not to add too many tricks.

sections.title: The EHLO Command
sections.content:
A client that supports extensions starts the session with EHLO instead of HELO. The syntax is EHLO, a space, a domain and CRLF. The RFC amends RFC 821 so that a session may begin with either command. Once EHLO has succeeded, a later HELO or EHLO gets a 503 reply, and the client must not cache what it learned, so it asks again at the start of each session.

A successful reply uses code 250 and is normally multiline. The first line has the domain and an optional greeting, and each following line holds an EHLO keyword and optional parameters. Keywords are case-insensitive. Any keyword beginning with X is a local extension used by bilateral agreement, and a conforming server must not offer a keyword without an X unless it is a registered, standardized extension.

If the server cannot list its extensions it returns 554. Other failures are 501 (bad argument), 502 (recognized but not implemented) and 421 (service no longer available). After any failure the client should issue HELO or QUIT.
sections.eli5: The client says 'EHLO, here is who I am.' The server answers with a list of its special skills, one per line, and the client checks which ones it can use.

sections.title: Servers Without Extensions
sections.content:
An RFC 821 server that does not know EHLO will answer with code 500 and should stay in the same state. The client may then send HELO or QUIT. Nothing breaks for old servers, which is why the framework needs no changes to servers that do not use it.

The RFC also mentions badly behaved servers. Some close the connection on EHLO, which violates RFC 821, so clients are advised to check for closure and, if the job can be done without extensions, reconnect and use HELO. Others refuse HELO after a rejected EHLO. Sending RSET first can sometimes work around that, and a failure code such as 503 in reply to the RSET can be ignored.
sections.eli5: If the other computer is old and does not understand the fancy hello, it says so, and you just use the plain hello you always used.

sections.title: The Registry and Command Parameters
sections.content:
The IANA keeps the registry of standard SMTP service extensions. Each entry is defined by a standards-track RFC and gives the extension's name, its EHLO keyword, parameter syntax, any new verbs, any new MAIL FROM or RCPT TO parameters, and how it changes client and server behavior. The initial registry holds SEND, SOML, SAML, EXPN, HELP and TURN, which are the optional commands already defined in RFC 821.

MAIL FROM and RCPT TO can now carry esmtp-parameters of the form keyword or keyword=value. All such keywords must be registered, and RFC 1651 itself defines none. A server that does not recognize or cannot implement a parameter returns 555, and a temporary inability returns 455 unless the parameter's definition says otherwise.

Servers also add a with ESMTP clause to the Received: header when any extension is used.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of the extra skills a mail computer can have, so everyone uses the same name for the same skill.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not discuss security issues and says it is not believed to raise any beyond those already present in electronic mail and in fully conforming RFC 821 implementations. The EHLO reply does announce server capabilities, but the RFC says everything announced by the initial extensions could be deduced by probing the verbs needed to transport and deliver mail.

Security implications of other extensions are to be handled in the RFCs that define them.
sections.eli5: The list of skills a server shares is something a curious visitor could find out by trying things anyway, so telling it is not a new danger.
